title: S&P 500 Closes at Record High as Tame Inflation Data Eases Rate-Hike Fears
excerpt: Flat producer prices in July helped push the benchmark index to 7,798.99, while oil dropped more than 2% and Treasury yields fell as traders scaled back September rate-hike bets.
body:
• The S&P 500 rose 0.65% to close at 7,798.99, surpassing its prior record set last Friday
  • U.S. Producer Price Index was unchanged in July, reinforcing softening inflation trends after a tame CPI report earlier in the week
  • Traders now price in a 63% chance the Fed holds rates steady in September, up from 50% on Wednesday
  • Oil prices dropped more than 2% despite Middle East tensions, as OPEC cut demand forecasts and U.S. crude inventories surged

Tech and Memory Chips Lead the Charge

The S&P 500 notched a fresh record-high close on Thursday, fueled by gains in technology and memory chip stocks after benign wholesale inflation data strengthened expectations that the Federal Reserve will not raise interest rates next month.

The benchmark index climbed 50.49 points, or 0.65%, to 7,798.99. The Nasdaq Composite added 214.54 points, or 0.81%, to 26,803.03, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 69.72 points, or 0.13%, to 53,839.99, closing within 1% of its own record.

Memory chip maker SanDisk surged 13.7% and Micron Technology gained 4.2%, while Meta Platforms rose 2.8% and Microsoft added nearly 1%. Netflix climbed 5.4% after billionaire investor Bill Ackman unveiled a new stake in the streaming company as part of Pershing Square's biggest portfolio overhaul in years, according to Reuters.

"The AI earnings-driven tech boom continues. It's an earnings boom, not a bubble."

— Jay Hatfield, CEO, Infrastructure Capital Advisors

Seven of the 11 S&P 500 sector indexes advanced, led by communication services, up 1.56%, followed by real estate with a 1.34% gain. On the losing side, Cisco Systems dropped 8.4% after its upbeat revenue forecast failed to satisfy investors with elevated expectations, and Tapestry plunged more than 16% on a muted annual revenue growth outlook.

Inflation Data Shifts the Rate Calculus

The U.S. Producer Price Index was unchanged in July from June, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported, as goods prices fell and the cost of services increased only marginally. The data followed a consumer-price index report earlier in the week that also pointed to moderating inflation.

Traders responded by scaling back September rate-hike bets. Fed funds futures now price in a 63% probability that the central bank will hold rates steady at its next meeting, up from roughly 50% on Wednesday, according to CME's FedWatch tool.

"Earnings season for AI infrastructure names has been strong and shows no signs of slowdown in capex," said Mohit Kumar, an economist at Jefferies. "The background of high amounts of cash in the system and Fed not hiking should continue to support risky assets."

The yield on the benchmark 10-year Treasury note fell 7.29 basis points to 4.619%, while the 30-year bond yield dropped 6 basis points to 5.187%. The dollar index edged down 0.1% to 99.85.

Oil Retreats Despite Strait of Hormuz Tensions

Crude oil prices fell sharply despite the continuing standoff over the Strait of Hormuz. Brent crude futures dropped about 2% to $87.07 a barrel, while U.S.-traded oil futures declined $2.02, or 2.4%, to $81.25.

The selloff came after U.S. commercial crude oil inventories posted their largest weekly gain since January 2023, and the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries lowered its world oil demand growth forecast for 2026, according to Reuters.

Washington and Tehran traded accusations over a deal to reopen the strategically vital waterway, with the United States saying Iran had failed to meet its obligations and Iran countering that Washington had not delivered on ending a blockade of Iranian ports.

Market Breadth and Outlook

Advancing issues outnumbered declining ones within the S&P 500 by a 1.7-to-one ratio. The index posted 30 new 52-week highs and just one new low. Volume was relatively light at 16.1 billion shares, below the 20-session average of 17.5 billion.

Year to date, the S&P 500 is up about 14%, while the Nasdaq has gained roughly 15%. Strong corporate earnings — particularly from AI infrastructure companies including Microsoft and Amazon — have continued to underpin investor optimism, even as geopolitical risks and fiscal concerns linger.

Analysts cautioned that the rally could face headwinds. "I would still be careful chasing rallies, especially in the back end, where supply, fiscal concerns and oil-related term premium remain hard to dismiss," said Mizuho strategist Evelyne Gomez-Liechti.
